This measure models the use of smart thermostats to achieve demand flexibility in residential buildings by controlling their heating and cooling systems. This document describes the technology in general, describes how it is modeled in ResStock™, and reviews results at a high level. 1.1 Introduction to Technology According to Stewart (2023): A smart thermostat is an internet-connected device that controls home heating, ventilation, and air-conditioning (HVAC) equipment and can automatically adjust temperature set points to optimize performance and achieve energy savings. Smart thermostat features often include two-way communication, occupancy detection (such as geofencing and occupancy sensors), schedule learning, and seasonal optimization algorithms. Smart thermostats can control most conventional HVAC systems including central air conditioners, heat pumps, and forced air furnaces. Within the context of demand flexibility programs, the internet-connected feature of a smart thermostat is used by the utility (with customer consent) to remotely adjust the thermostat set points during target times. For example, Xcel Energy deploys Ecobee smart thermostats in their 2 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR) at www.nlr.gov/publications. demand response program. These thermostats adjust customer home cooling set points by 1°F– 4°F for up to 4 hours when there is a risk of an electricity shortage, as determined by Xcel Energy. 1.2 Technical Measure Details Demand flexibility is commonly categorized into four groups: load shaping, load shifting, load shedding, and load shimmying (Peter Alstone, 2017). In this analysis, we consider load shifting and load shedding. In the following discussion, the peak period, or “on-peak window,” is the window of time when the peak is to be reduced. The pre-peak window is the window of time immediately preceding the peak period. 1.2.1 Load Shifting As defined in (Peter Alstone, 2017), load shifting “represents DR [demand response] that encourages the movement of energy consumption from times of high demand to times when there is a surplus of renewable generation. Shift could smooth net load ramps associated with daily patterns of solar energy generation.” For this analysis, load shifting is accomplished by preheating (for heating days) or precooling (for cooling days) the building prior to the on-peak window (during the pre-peak window). The idea is that the preheating or precooling increases the load prior to the on-peak window, conditions the indoor air, and preconditions the thermal mass and air in the building. Then the building requires less heating or cooling energy to maintain the set point during the on-peak window, reducing the overall load profile during this window. The extent of the load reduction will depend on the building’s characteristics, such as the thermal mass, the amount of insulation, the infiltration, the duration of the preconditioning, and the timing of the peak period. 1.2.2 Load Shedding As defined in (Peter Alstone, 2017), load shedding “describes loads that can be curtailed to provide peak capacity and support the system in emergency or contingency events.” For this analysis, load shedding is
